claims.text: A machine-learning approach integrating composition-based descriptors and phonon-scattering metrics can more reliably identify high-entropy alloys with low phonon thermal conductivity.
The proposed approach will achieve 10–20% lower prediction error than conventional first-principles or empirical models.
The target materials are high-entropy alloys containing 4–6 principal elements in near-equiatomic or moderately concentrated compositions.
The model will be trained to correlate compositional and microstructural attributes with experimentally measured thermal conductivity.
Laser-flash analysis or time-domain thermoreflectance will be used to validate the model.
In the 400–800 K range, phonon scattering effects largely determine the lattice thermal conductivity of the target high-entropy alloys.
Multi-element configurations in high-entropy alloys produce increased lattice strain and atomic mass or size mismatch.
Lattice strain and atomic mass or size mismatch enhance phonon scattering.
Enhanced phonon scattering reduces thermal transport.
Learning relationships among composition, local atomic disorder, and phonon scattering allows the model to capture correlations missed by simpler empirical or purely ab initio approaches.
Capturing these complex correlations improves the accuracy of low-thermal-conductivity predictions.
Novel or underexplored alloys selected by the model will have significantly lower thermal conductivity in the 400–800 K range than existing predictions indicate.
The model's predictions for the selected alloys will agree more closely with measured thermal conductivity than existing predictions do.
Crude empirical rules, rule-of-mixtures models, and unrefined first-principles methods often have higher average thermal-conductivity prediction errors in multicomponent alloys.
The approach is applicable primarily to composition ranges that are sufficiently represented in its training data.
The model may be less reliable for extreme compositions outside the database or for sparsely sampled property regimes.
A lack of large thermal-transport datasets may limit the model's predictive power.
The exact improvement over existing predictions cannot be established without systematic benchmarks across multiple high-entropy-alloy families.
At least three newly predicted high-entropy-alloy compositions will be synthesized and tested from 400 to 800 K.
The hypothesis will be falsified if at least two tested alloys have measured thermal conductivities that differ by more than 20% from the model's predicted low values.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis gives a specific 10–20% error-reduction estimate, while the uncertainty field states that the magnitude of improvement cannot be stated definitively without further systematic benchmarking.
